gaps.sentence: The discussion got to a stage ___ nobody was listening any more.
gaps.explanation: 'A stage where ...' means 'a stage at which ...'; the clause has its own subject and verb, so 'which' is impossible.

gaps.sentence: The winner, ___ was only seventeen, broke the championship record.
gaps.hint: person as subject after a comma
gaps.explanation: The clause adds extra information about a person, so 'who' is required and 'that' is impossible.

gaps.sentence: Have you got anything ___ will remove this stain?
gaps.explanation: After 'anything', 'that' is the preferred relative pronoun; 'which' is avoided after -thing words.

gaps.sentence: She was two hours late, ___ annoyed the interviewer.
gaps.hint: comment on the whole situation before the comma
gaps.explanation: When a clause comments on the whole previous statement, use 'which' after the comma.

gaps.sentence: Nobody knows the reason ___ he resigned so suddenly.
gaps.explanation: 'The reason why ...' is the standard pattern; 'why' means 'for which'.

gaps.sentence: They said nothing at all, ___ I found rather strange.
gaps.explanation: 'Which' here means 'and this'; it refers to the whole situation and follows a comma.

gaps.sentence: The director, ___ we met at the conference, has written to us.
gaps.hint: person as object, but the clause is non-defining
gaps.explanation: In non-defining clauses 'that' cannot replace 'who', even when the person is the object.

gaps.sentence: Mrs Patterson, ___ taught me maths, has just retired.
gaps.hint: extra information after a comma about a person
gaps.explanation: After a comma the relative clause is non-defining, so 'that' is impossible and 'who' refers to the person.
